headline.statement: The trial's conclusion that prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis "may not be necessary" rests on five infection events in total, with no confidence interval or effect estimate reported anywhere, and on the least conservative of three available tests -- the exact test appropriate to a table this sparse returns p = 1.000.
headline.evidence: "There were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group" (n = 28 per arm). "According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference ... (p = 0.639)." Recomputed from those counts: Pearson χ² = 0.2196, df = 1, p = 0.639339 -- matching the printed value exactly -- but with expected cell counts of 2.5 in both infection cells. Fisher's exact test on the identical table gives p = 1.000 and an odds ratio of 1.56; Yates-corrected χ² gives p = 1.000. No confidence interval, risk difference or effect size appears anywhere in the paper.
headline.plain: The study found 3 infections in one group of 28 patients and 2 in the other, then concluded that carrying on antibiotics after surgery may be unnecessary. With only five infections in total the study simply cannot tell a real difference from chance, and it never reports how large a difference its data would still allow. The arithmetic behind the number it does report is correct, but the more appropriate test for such small counts returns a result that is completely uninformative.

findings.title: Null conclusion about antibiotic prophylaxis reported with no confidence interval, risk difference or effect size
findings.location: Results, final paragraph; Discussion, final paragraph; Abstract (Results and Conclusion)
findings.reported: "According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639)." "Therefore, prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections." No confidence interval, risk difference or effect size is printed for this comparison anywhere in the paper.
findings.computed: The check designed for exactly this claim, absence_of_evidence, could not be run: it requires an interval, or a coefficient with a standard error, and the paper prints neither. The only effect estimate recoverable is the odds ratio of 1.56 that recalc_chi_squared returns from the reconstructed 2x2 table (3/28 versus 2/28), and no registered tool produces a confidence interval around an odds ratio from cell counts. With 3 and 2 events in arms of 28 that interval would in any case be very wide. The largest difference the data still permit is therefore unquantified, and "not significant" cannot be read as "no difference".
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The event counts and arm sizes are the paper's; the odds ratio of 1.56 is computed by a registered tool from those counts.

consequence.explanation: The paper's central conclusion -- that prolonged prophylaxis may be unnecessary -- is stated without any quantification of the difference the study was unable to rule out.

findings.plain: The authors say there was no significant difference in infection rates, and conclude that continuing antibiotics after surgery may be unnecessary. But a finding of "no significant difference" only means the study did not detect one; it does not mean there is none. To judge that, a reader needs to know how big a difference the data could still be hiding, and the paper never provides that figure. With three infections in one group and two in the other, the range of differences still compatible with these results is very wide.

findings.title: Chi-squared test applied to a table with expected counts of 2.5; the exact test on the same data returns p = 1.000
findings.location: Results, final paragraph; Patients and Methods, statistical analysis sentence
findings.reported: "Statistical analysis was performed using a χ²-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA)." The reported result is p = 0.639, with no chi-squared statistic and no degrees of freedom printed.
findings.computed: Rebuilding the 2x2 table from the printed counts (3/28 versus 2/28) gives expected cell counts of 2.5 in both infection cells, below the conventional minimum of 5 for the chi-squared approximation. The uncorrected Pearson test the paper used returns χ² = 0.2196, df = 1, p = 0.639339, which rounds exactly to the printed 0.639 -- so the arithmetic is correct for the test named. Fisher's exact test and the Yates-corrected chi-squared both return p = 1.000 on the identical table. The paper reports the least conservative of the three conventions without noting that a correction or exact test was considered, and SPSS 12.0 prints the Fisher exact p and a minimum-expected-count warning automatically for a 2x2 of this size.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The 2x2 table is reconstructed entirely from counts the paper prints (3 and 2 infections, 28 per arm).

consequence.explanation: All three conventions are far from significance, so the direction of the conclusion is unchanged; what changes is how much information the reported p conveys, since the appropriate exact test is completely uninformative at p = 1.000.

findings.plain: The statistical test the authors used assumes each cell of the comparison contains at least about five cases; here the expected number was 2.5. The test better suited to such small numbers gives a result of exactly 1.000 -- meaning the data say nothing at all about whether the groups differ. The number the paper reports, 0.639, is correctly calculated for the test they chose, but it makes the comparison look more informative than it is. Either way the answer is the same: no difference was detected.

findings.title: Unblinded outcome assessment by the operating surgeon, with a placebo referred to but never given
findings.reported: "A horizontal maxillary osteotomy and vertical ramus mandibular osteotomy were performed by the same oral surgeon." "The patients in the experimental group received only 1.0 g of a third-generation cephalosporin (Cefpiramide) intravenously 30 minutes before surgery and did not receive the placebo." Postoperative infection was assessed against CDC surgical site infection criteria, one of which is diagnosis by the surgeon or attending physician. No blinding of patients, surgeon or outcome assessors is described.
findings.computed: A design reading, not a calculation: an unblinded two-arm trial with no placebo, in which all operations were performed by one surgeon and one of the four outcome criteria is that surgeon's own diagnosis. Outcome ascertainment was therefore open and partly subjective. The phrase "did not receive the placebo" uses the definite article for a placebo the paper never otherwise mentions, which reads as residue from an earlier protocol or draft in which one was planned.
findings.assumptions: CONSORT 2001 (the version current when this 2009 paper was written) item 11 asks whether participants, those administering the intervention and those assessing outcomes were blinded; the paper does not claim to follow CONSORT, so this is an external standard applied to a trial report. Note the direction: open assessment would if anything bias toward finding a difference, and none was found, so this weakens the paper's ability to support a null conclusion rather than manufacturing a positive one.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a reading of the Methods section, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: Bears on how much weight the null conclusion about postoperative prophylaxis can carry, without changing any reported number.

findings.plain: Everyone involved knew which patients were getting extra antibiotics -- there was no dummy treatment, and the same surgeon operated on all patients and also helped decide who counted as infected. Knowing who got what can influence such judgements. Here the effect would most likely push toward finding a difference, and none was found, so this does not undermine the reported result; it does limit how confidently the absence of a difference can be interpreted.

findings.title: Sample-size justification labels the Type II error rate as the study's power
findings.reported: "Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of α= 0.05 and a test power β= 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%."
findings.computed: Beta denotes the Type II error rate; statistical power is 1 minus beta. A beta of 0.20 corresponds to a power of 0.80, so 0.20 is not the power. As printed, the sentence asserts a power of 0.20. Separately, the calculation itself could not be reproduced: verify_power_analysis for two proportions requires a standardised effect size (Cohen's h), the paper states two raw proportions (5% and 5% + 30%), and no registered tool converts a proportion pair to h.
findings.assumptions: The conventional reading -- beta = 0.20, hence 80% power -- is almost certainly what the authors did, and under that reading nothing numeric is wrong. This is recorded because the sentence is the paper's entire justification for its sample size and cannot be resolved from the paper alone. Note also that a design powered to detect 5% versus 35% is powered for a 30-percentage-point difference, far larger than the 10.7% versus 7.1% actually observed.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a reading of statistical notation in the paper's text, and the underlying power calculation is not reproducible because no registered tool converts the paper's two proportions (0.05 and 0.35) into Cohen's h.

consequence.explanation: Affects the interpretation of the sample-size justification only; under the conventional reading (power = 0.80) no reported result changes.

findings.plain: The paper explains its choice of 28 patients per group by citing what it calls a "test power" of 0.20. In standard usage that symbol means the chance of missing a real effect, so 0.20 corresponds to a power of 80 per cent, not 20. The authors almost certainly meant the standard thing, but as written the sentence says the opposite. More importantly, the calculation was aimed at detecting a difference of 30 percentage points in infection rates -- an enormous effect -- so the study was never designed to detect the smaller differences that actually matter here.

findings.title: Reported age dispersion is inconsistent with a cohort described as "in their 20s", and no age range is printed
findings.location: Patients and Methods, paragraph 1; Results, paragraph 1; Table 1, Age row
findings.reported: "Fifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history ... were enrolled in this study." "The mean (SD) age of the experimental group was 23.9 years (5.84)." "The mean (SD) age of the control group was 24.3 years (6.33)." No minimum, maximum or age range is printed anywhere.
findings.computed: For data confined to ages 20 to 30, the largest attainable standard deviation is 5.09. The reported SDs of 5.84 and 6.33 are 1.15 and 1.24 times that ceiling. Reading the values as standard errors instead makes matters worse (implied SDs of 30.9 and 33.5), so neither dispersion interpretation fits a strictly 20-to-29 cohort.
findings.assumptions: THE BOUND IS MINE, NOT THE PAPER'S. The 20-to-30 ceiling is my translation of the phrase "in their 20s"; the paper prints no numerals for an age range, so under rulebook rule 4 this is an assumed bound and the finding is capped at suspicious and cannot be the headline. The likeliest innocent explanation is that "in their 20s" is loose descriptive prose for a predominantly young cohort rather than an eligibility criterion, in which case the SDs are unremarkable and nothing is wrong. The paper is silent on which it is -- so what is reportable here is the missing age range, not an arithmetic defect. Working against the innocent reading, the Discussion criticises prior studies for a "wide range of patient's age", which would be self-defeating if this study's own range were broad; but that is an inference, not a stated bound.

consequence.explanation: Age is a baseline descriptor only; it enters no reported test, so no claim in the paper depends on the age figures being right.

findings.plain: The paper describes its patients as being in their twenties, but the spread it reports around the average age of about 24 is too wide for a group all aged 20 to 29 -- it implies a substantial number of patients younger than 20 or older than 30. The most likely explanation is simply that "in their 20s" was casual wording rather than an entry rule, and the paper never states the actual youngest and oldest ages, so this cannot be settled from the article. Nothing in the study's conclusions depends on it.

findings.title: No participant-flow statement: complete follow-up of all 56 patients is inferred, never stated
findings.location: Patients and Methods, paragraph 2; Table 1 column headers
findings.reported: "The 56 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the randomization codes generated by Microsoft Excel: an experimental and control group." Table 1 reports 28 patients per arm. No withdrawals, losses to follow-up, protocol deviations or post-randomisation exclusions are reported anywhere.
findings.computed: That all 56 randomised patients were analysed is an inference from the two arm sizes summing to the enrolled total (28 + 28 = 56, verified at zero tolerance), not a statement the paper makes.
findings.assumptions: CONSORT 2001 item 13 (participant flow) is an external standard the paper does not claim to follow. Graded indeterminate rather than as a red flag because complete follow-up is entirely plausible here: the outcome window is two weeks, assessment occurred at scheduled postoperative visits during an inpatient and early-postoperative period, and the patients were young and healthy. Rulebook rule 7 concerns implausibly low dropout over long horizons and does not fit a two-week surgical follow-up. What is missing is the statement, not necessarily the retention.

consequence.explanation: No reported number changes; the analysed sample simply cannot be confirmed independently of the arithmetic inference.

findings.plain: The paper never says whether any of the 56 patients dropped out or missed their follow-up appointments. That all of them completed the study is deduced from the group sizes adding up, not from anything the authors wrote. Over a two-week window after surgery, complete follow-up is entirely believable; the point is that a reader has to assume it.
findings.reproduction_problem: THE COMMAND DISAGREES WITH THE FINDING: it reports `consistent` where the finding claims `indeterminate`. The command ran perfectly well -- that is the point. Re-read the finding before the paper.

not_checked.location: Discussion, sample-size paragraph (alpha 0.05, beta 0.20, rates 5% and 5% + 30%, n = 28 per group)

not_checked.reason: GRIM was run on both group mean ages and refused both times. The paper also never states that age was recorded in whole years. No inference about the ages can be drawn from this check in either direction.

csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion were deliberately not run, so the rulebook's baseline-similarity signature could not be evaluated in either direction. Both require baseline p-values or per-row group statistics across several independent baseline variables; this trial reports no baseline p-values at all and has only two baseline rows, one of which (sex) is a pair of counts. Two rows cannot support a dispersion estimate, and fabricating baseline p-values would manufacture the input. The near-identical ages (23.9 versus 24.3) and sex splits across arms are therefore neither flagged nor cleared here.

Zero of five was a real weakness in the evidence.

This system reads one paper and reaches no network. Two questions a reader would want answered about the age-dispersion finding -- whether similar tensions appear in other papers by these authors, and what age ranges comparable orthognathic trials report -- are outside its reach entirely.

No registered tool converts a pair of proportions into Cohen's h, so the paper's stated a-priori power calculation could not be reproduced at all. Likewise, no registered tool computes a confidence interval for an odds ratio from 2x2 cell counts, so the imprecision of the primary null result could be described but not quantified. Both are gaps in our toolkit, not in the paper.

The rulebook's baseline-similarity test (rule 1: uniformly high baseline p-values as a red flag) could not be applied. This trial reports no baseline p-values and has only two baseline rows, which cannot support the omnibus methods. The very close baseline ages across arms are therefore neither flagged nor cleared.

questions_for_authors.question: Your Results give the primary comparison as "no significant difference ... (p = 0.639)" from 3 infections of 28 and 2 of 28. Could you send the effect estimate and its 95% confidence interval for that comparison -- the risk difference or the relative risk -- so that readers can see how large a difference the data still permit?
questions_for_authors.why: The paper's central conclusion is a null claim supported only by a p-value; the interval is what determines whether "no significant difference" can support "may not be necessary".

questions_for_authors.question: The infection table has expected cell counts of 2.5, and on those same counts Fisher's exact test and the Yates-corrected chi-squared both return p = 1.000 while the uncorrected Pearson test returns the p = 0.639 you report. Could you confirm which SPSS output line the reported value was taken from, and whether an exact test was also examined?
questions_for_authors.why: Establishes whether the least conservative convention was chosen deliberately or is simply the default line of the SPSS crosstabs output.

questions_for_authors.question: Your Patients and Methods describe "fifty-six patients in their 20s", while the reported age dispersion is 23.9 (SD 5.84) and 24.3 (SD 6.33). Could you supply the minimum and maximum age in each arm, so that the age range of the enrolled cohort is on record?
questions_for_authors.why: Would settle in one line whether "in their 20s" was an eligibility criterion or descriptive prose, which is the whole of the age finding.

questions_for_authors.question: The sample-size paragraph states "a significance level of α= 0.05 and a test power β= 0.20". Could you confirm that the target power was 0.80 (that is, β = 0.20 as the Type II error rate), and send the tail convention used, so the calculation giving 28 per group can be reproduced?
questions_for_authors.why: The sentence as printed asserts a power of 0.20; confirming the intended reading and the tail convention would make the sample-size justification reproducible.

questions_for_authors.question: Your Methods state that experimental-group patients "did not receive the placebo". Could you clarify whether a placebo was planned at protocol stage, and whether the surgeon and patients were aware of group allocation when postoperative infection was assessed?
questions_for_authors.why: The definite article implies a placebo arm that is never otherwise described; blinding status bears directly on how the null result should be weighted.

report_markdown:
This is a small prospective randomised trial from a Korean university dental hospital. Fifty-six patients undergoing Le Fort I osteotomy with bilateral intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy were allocated by Excel-generated codes into two arms of 28: one receiving a single preoperative dose of cefpiramide, the other the same dose plus twice-daily continuation to day 3. Patients were followed for two weeks against CDC surgical site infection criteria. Three infections occurred in the single-dose arm and two in the continued arm, and the authors conclude that prolonged postoperative prophylaxis "may not be necessary".

**What reconciles.** The arithmetic in this paper holds up well, and that is worth stating precisely rather than in passing. Every count adds up at zero tolerance: the sex splits sum to their arm sizes (16 + 12 = 28, 14 + 14 = 28) and the arms sum to the 56 patients enrolled. The case-by-case narrative of the infected patients -- one maxillary presentation plus four mandibular -- totals five, matching the 3 + 2 printed in Table 1, and the single case of wound dehiscence matches the table too. The sex ratios given in the prose as "4 : 3" and "1 : 1" correspond to the counts in the table. Most importantly, the paper's single inferential result reproduces exactly: rebuilding the 2x2 from the printed counts and running an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared returns p = 0.639339, which rounds to the printed 0.639. Seven of the twelve checks that reached a verdict passed, and the one number the paper's conclusion depends on is among them. There is no sign anywhere of the anomalies this kind of analysis exists to detect.

**Where the difficulty lies, and it is not in the arithmetic.** The problem with this paper is what it asks five events to carry. The comparison is 3 of 28 against 2 of 28. On the test appropriate to a table with expected cell counts of 2.5 -- Fisher's exact, which SPSS 12.0 prints automatically alongside a minimum-expected-count warning for a 2x2 of this size -- the answer is p = 1.000: the data are entirely uninformative about whether the groups differ. The paper instead reports the uncorrected Pearson value of 0.639. That value is correctly computed for the test named, and every convention here is far from significance, so no conclusion changes. What changes is how much information the reported number appears to convey.

That would matter less if the paper quantified what it could not rule out. It does not. There is no confidence interval, no risk difference and no effect size anywhere in the article for the primary comparison, which is why the check designed for precisely this situation could not be run at all. The only effect estimate recoverable is an odds ratio of 1.56 from the reconstructed table, and nothing in this toolkit puts an interval around it from cell counts. So a reader is asked to move from "not significant" to "may not be necessary" without being shown the range of differences the data still permit -- and with five events across 56 patients, that range is very wide.

The paper's own sample-size paragraph makes this explicit without meaning to. It was designed to detect a difference of 30 percentage points, from 5% to 35%. The rates actually observed were 10.7% and 7.1%. A design tuned to an effect that large has, by construction, almost no ability to detect the smaller differences that would actually matter clinically. The same sentence labels 0.20 as "a test power" when 0.20 is the Type II error rate -- almost certainly a notation slip for 80% power, but it sits in the one sentence that justifies the sample size, and a reader cannot resolve it from the article.

**The finding I am least sure of, and why.** The reported age dispersion -- 23.9 (SD 5.84) and 24.3 (SD 6.33) -- is wider than a cohort confined to ages 20 to 29 could produce; the ceiling for that decade is 5.09. But that ceiling is my translation of the phrase "in their 20s", and the paper prints no age range at all. The likeliest reading is that the phrase was descriptive prose rather than an eligibility rule, in which case nothing is wrong. This repository's own rulebook names that exact phrase as a documented route to a false accusation, so it is capped and it is not the headline. What is genuinely reportable is narrower: the age range of the enrolled cohort is not on record, and one line from the authors would settle it.

**Two things a reader should carry, neither a defect in the numbers.** The trial was unblinded with no placebo, all operations were performed by one surgeon, and one of the four CDC criteria is that surgeon's own diagnosis -- though the direction matters here, since open assessment would if anything bias toward finding a difference, and none was found. And there is no participant-flow statement: that all 56 patients completed follow-up is deduced from the arm sizes summing to the total, not stated. Over a two-week postoperative window that is entirely believable, and I record it as unresolved rather than as a flag.

The numbers in this paper reconcile with each other. What I cannot settle is whether they support the conclusion drawn from them, because the paper does not report the quantity that would decide it.
